# Instruction Set Architecture

This chapter describes the MISA instruction set architecture, including the base instruction set,
optional assembler extensions, special registers and hardware data structures, and other
implementation-agnostic features.

The MISA architecture is an 8-bit architecture with up to a 16-bit address bus to interface with
externally connected memory. Instructions are fixed-width 16-bit doublewords in little-endian byte
order.

The information presented in this chapter is referred to as the MISA core architecture. The last
section of this chapter enumerates several optional extensions to the core architecture, although
an implementation is considered conforming if it implements at least the core architecture.

## General Purpose Registers

The general-purpose register file contains sixteen, 8-bit registers for general computation and
data storage, defined by the following ABI:

| ABI Name    | ABI Purpose               | Wide ABI Name | Encoding |
|-------------|---------------------------|---------------|----------|
| `R0`        | Hard-wired zero           | N/A           | 0000     |
| `RA`        | Argument/temporary        | `RAB`         | 0001     |
| `RB`        | Argument/temporary        |               | 0010     |
| `RC`        | Argument/temporary        | `RCD`         | 0011     |
| `RD`        | Argument/temporary        |               | 0100     |
| `RE`        | Argument/temporary        | `REF`         | 0101     |
| `RF`        | Argument/temporary        |               | 0110     |
| `RU`        | Saved                     | `RUV`         | 0111     |
| `RV`        | Saved                     |               | 1000     |
| `RW`        | Saved                     | `RWX`         | 1001     |
| `RX`        | Saved                     |               | 1010     |
| `RY`        | Saved                     | `RYZ`         | 1011     |
| `RZ`        | Saved                     |               | 1100     |
| `RT`        | Argument/return/temporary | N/A           | 1101     |
| `RSCRATCH0` | Assembler scratch         | `RSCRATCH`    | 1110     |
| `RSCRATCH1` | Assembler scratch         |               | 1111     |

The `R0` register must be hard-wired to ignore writes and always return the value `0b00000000` on
reads. Wide registers are formed by two general-purpose registers, which must be equivalent to
using the two 8-bit register names in order. For instance, `RAB` is semantically equivalent to
`RA, RB` in that order. General purpose registers can be taken as the operands to most instructions
which operate on registers.

Argument and return registers are `RA` - `RF` and `RT`. The `RT` register should be used as the
first return register, if the value being returned logically fits in a single (not wide) register.
Otherwise, the register pair `RAB` should be preferred as the first return register. Argument
registers are also temporary registers (caller-saved). `RU` through `RZ` are saved registers
(callee-saved).

The `RSCRATCH` wide register is reserved as a "scratch" 16-bit register for the assembler. Certain
pseudo-instructions and other macros will use this register when a temporary value is needed (like
loading an address to jump to). As such, the value of `RSCRATCH` should not be assumed to persist
over time.

## Control and Status Registers

Also required are a few special registers, which cannot be used as instruction operands, but can
be read and written from general purpose registers with the `RSR` and `WSR` instructions. Special
registers are generally wider 16-bit registers that are required for the operation of certain
instructions.

When used as operands for instructions, the special registers are encoded as follows:

| ABI Name | Encoding                           |
|----------|------------------------------------|
| `SADDR`  | 0001                               |
| `RADDR`  | 0010                               |
| `FLAGS`  | 0011                               |
| `CAUSE`  | 0100                               |
| `EXTNS`  | 0101                               |
| `RETSC`  | 1000 (under System Call Extension) |
| `RETIR`  | 1001 (under Interrupt Extension)   |
| `PRIVS`  | 1010 (under Privilege Extension)   |

The following sub-sections describe the purpose and layout of each special register.

### `SADDR`

The stack address or stack pointer. `SADDR` must be at least an 8-bit register (supporting stack
addresses `0x00` - `0xFF` with a possible high 8-bit prefix) and no more than a 16-bit register.

```{python}
#| echo: false
import wavedrom
from IPython.display import SVG
SVG(wavedrom.render(str({
    "reg": [
        {"name": "SADDR LO (required)", "bits": 8},
        {"name": "SADDR HI (optional)", "bits": 8}
    ],
    "config": {"bits": 16}
})).tostring())
```

### `RADDR`

The return address is also a dedicated special register given the limited number of general
purpose registers available. `RADDR` is required to be wide enough to store an absolute address
for the connected memory, which generally means 16-bit.

The return address special register is not used by specific base instructions, but provides a
dedicated 16-bit-wide register for subroutine calling. The `JAL` instruction will set the
`RADDR` register with the address of the instruction after the `JAL`. Returning to the location
in `RADDR` can be done with a `RSR` and `JMP` or a `JMP` using `RADDR` as the branch target.

```{python}
#| echo: false
import wavedrom
from IPython.display import SVG
SVG(wavedrom.render(str({
    "reg": [
        {"name": "RADDR", "bits": 16},
    ],
    "config": {"bits": 16}
})).tostring())
```

### `FLAGS`

Conditional branching in the MISA architecture is based on ALU flag values for comparing integers.
Both branching instructions, `JAL` and `JMP`, use these flags to make decisions on whether a branch
will be taken.

`FLAGS` is set based on the result of each ALU operation. The instructions which must update
the `FLAGS` register are: `ADD`, `ADC`, `SUB`, `SBB`, `RRC`. Instructions which may, depending on
the implementation, update the `FLAGS` register are: `HALT`, `AND`, `OR`, `XOR`. Instructions which
must not update the `FLAGS` register are: `SET`, `LD`, `ST`, `RSR`, `WSR` (must not update `FLAGS`
asynchronously through the ALU output, but will update `FLAGS` if writing directly to it), `JAL`,
`JMP`. A conditional branch that relies on `FLAGS` should be performed immediately after the
conditional comparison or a `WSR` to `FLAGS`.

The `FLAGS` special register is a flags register (one bit per flag) which must be at least 4 bits
and support the following:

| Flag | Bit | Commentary                                                           |
|------|-----|----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `Z`  | 0   | Whether the last ALU operation's output was zero.                    |
| `C`  | 1   | The adder carry out bit of the last ALU operation.                   |
| `N`  | 2   | Whether the last ALU operation's output was negative (MSB = 1).      |
| `V`  | 3   | Whether the last ALU operation's output overflowed (sign inversion). |

```{python}
#| echo: false
import wavedrom
from IPython.display import SVG
SVG(wavedrom.render(str({
    "reg": [
        {"name": "Z", "bits": 1},
        {"name": "C", "bits": 1},
        {"name": "N", "bits": 1},
        {"name": "V", "bits": 1},
        {"name": "Reserved (optional)", "bits": 12}
    ],
    "config": {"bits": 16}
})).tostring())
```

The `FLAGS` register can be accessed indirectly with the conditional jump instructions using
special assembler symbols:

| ABI Name        | Logical Meaning  | Encoding |
|-----------------|------------------|----------|
| `ALWAYS`        | `1`              | 000      |
| `EQUAL`         | `Z`              | 001      |
| `NOT_EQUAL`     | `~Z`             | 010      |
| `GREATER`       | `~((N ^ V) | Z)` | 011      |
| `LESS`          | `N ^ V`          | 100      |
| `GREATER_EQUAL` | `~(N ^ V)`       | 101      |
| `LESS_EQUAL`    | `(N ^ V) | Z`    | 110      |

These comparison flags, when passed as a conditional branch instruction operand, must perform
the specified boolean logic on the fields of the `FLAGS` register. If the result is `1`, the
branch is taken, otherwise the branch is not taken. The assumption is that a comparison of
registers `RS1` and `RS2` is performed by invoking `SUB R0 RS1 RS2`, which sets the ALU flags
appropriately for deciding `RS1 ? RS2` where `?` is a comparison operator.

### `CAUSE`

The `CAUSE` special register holds information about the status of the processor during exceptions,
faults, and termination. It is set when the `HALT` instruction is executed, when syscalls are made
under the System Call Extension, and when fault behavior (such as a malformed instruction decode)
occurs during execution.

`CAUSE` is a 16-bit register with the following fields:

```{python}
#| echo: false
import wavedrom
from IPython.display import SVG
SVG(wavedrom.render(str({
    "reg": [
        {"name": "Reason", "bits": 3},
        {"name": "Type", "bits": 3},
        {"name": "Reserved", "bits": 2},
        {"name": "Extended status", "bits": 8}
    ],
    "config": {"bits": 16}
})).tostring())
```

| Reason            | Encoding |
|-------------------|----------|
| None              | 000      |
| Instruction usage | 001      |
| Memory usage      | 010      |
| Control event     | 011      |

#### `CAUSE` Reason: None
The `CAUSE` register does not represent an exception, or represents an unknown/generic exception
without a reason. If the reason is 000, the Type and Extended status fields have no significance.

#### `CAUSE` Reason: Instruction Usage
The exception cause is related to the use of a specific instruction or class of instructions. The
valid Type fields are:

| Type                   | Encoding | Commentary                                                                                                                                                                                          |
|------------------------|----------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Halt instruction       | 000      | The `HALT` instruction was executed. Extended status is the value of the `RS` operand register. Under the System Call Extension, this reason indicates that the `SYSCALL` instruction was executed. |
| Illegal instruction    | 001      | An ill-formed instruction failed to decode. Extended status is not used.                                                                                                                            |
| Privileged instruction | 010      | A privileged instruction was executed while in User Mode (under Privilege Extension).                                                                                                               |

: {tbl-colwidths="[20, 15, 65]"}

#### `CAUSE` Reason: Memory Usage
The exception cause is related to the use of an address or memory operation. The valid Type fields
are:

| Type              | Encoding | Commentary                                                                                   |
|-------------------|----------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Address overflow  | 000      | A memory operation attempted to access an address which is outside the mapped memory space.  |
| PC overflow       | 001      | The program counter overflowed an unsigned 16-bit value.                                     |
| Privileged access | 010      | An access to privileged memory was attempted while in User Mode (under Privilege Extension). |

: {tbl-colwidths="[20, 15, 65]"}

#### `CAUSE` Reason: Control Event
The exception cause is related to an exception or interrupt control flow event. The valid Type
fields are:

| Type                       | Encoding | Commentary                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
|----------------------------|----------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Improper return context    | 000      | Either: `JMP ALWAYS RETSC` was executed outside of a system call context or inside of an interrupt context; `JMP ALWAYS RETIR` was executed outside of an interrupt context. The extended status is set as follows: bit 0 = in system call context, bit 1 = in interrupt context, bits 2-3 = reserved, bits 4-7 = `JMP` target CSR register index. |
| Conditional context return | 001      | `JMP` was executed with a branch target of `RETSC` or `RETIR` but a comparison other than `ALWAYS`. The extended status is set as follows: bits 0-2 = comparison type, bit 3 = reserved, bits 4-7 = `JMP` target CSR register index.                                                                                                               |
| Improper system call       | 010      | A system call was executed while the processor was in a system call or interrupt context. The extended status is set as follows: bit 0 = in system call context, bit 1 = in interrupt context.                                                                                                                                                     |

: {tbl-colwidths="[20, 15, 65]"}

### `EXTNS`

The `EXTNS` special register is a flags register that holds information about which (if any)
architectural extensions are supported by the hardware. All implementations of the MISA
architecture must include the `EXTNS` register, even those which only implement the core
architecture. A core-only implementation can be identified by `EXTNS == 0x0000`.

Unlike most special registers, writes to `EXTNS` may be ignored (i.e. the register may have a
hard-coded value). For more information on writes to `EXTNS`, see the Dynamic Hardware Extension.
Note that bit 0 (the Dynamic Hardware Extension) *must* ignore writes regardless of its state,
preventing the Dynamic Hardware Extension from disabling itself.

`EXTNS` must support at least the following bits. A recommended width is 16-bits (with unsupported
extensions being forced to `0`), but the actual register width is implementation-defined. Unused
bits must always be read as zero and ignored on writes (if supported):

| Bit | Extension                  |
|-----|----------------------------|
| 0   | Dynamic Hardware Extension |
| 1   | System Call Extension      |
| 2   | Privilege Extension        |
| 3   | Interrupt Extension        |

## Data Formats and Alignments

The MISA architecture defined in this chapter only supports 8-bit signed integers using two's
complement encoding, where the value of an integer is given by the sum of its active bits:

```{python}
#| echo: false
import wavedrom
from IPython.display import SVG
SVG(wavedrom.render(str({
    "reg": [
        {"name": "1", "bits": 1},
        {"name": "2", "bits": 1},
        {"name": "4", "bits": 1},
        {"name": "8", "bits": 1},
        {"name": "16", "bits": 1},
        {"name": "32", "bits": 1},
        {"name": "64", "bits": 1},
        {"name": "-128", "bits": 1}
    ],
    "config": {"bits": 8}
})).tostring())
```

16-bit data types may be supported in software using the `ADC` and `SBB` instructions for
arithmetic.

## Memory

The MISA architecture supports up to a 16-bit address bus for memory operations, and memory must
be byte-addressable. While the memory map for applications using the MISA architecture is generally
free for the user to decide, this section will cover both a recommended map and specific regions
which are required by all maps.

### Required Memory Regions

The region 0xFFF0 - 0xFFFF is reserved for a reset vector table. When the processor is taken out of
reset, the program counter must be initialized to the address stored in memory at 0xFFFE - 0xFFFF
and begin execution there.

The reset vector table contains the following functions:

| Vector Address    | Purpose                                       |
|-------------------|-----------------------------------------------|
| `0xFFF0 - 0xFFF1` | Reserved                                      |
| `0xFFF2 - 0xFFF3` | Reserved                                      |
| `0xFFF4 - 0xFFF5` | Reserved                                      |
| `0xFFF6 - 0xFFF7` | Reserved                                      |
| `0xFFF8 - 0xFFF9` | Interrupt handler (under Interrupt Extension) |
| `0xFFFA - 0xFFFB` | Syscall handler (under System Call Extension) |
| `0xFFFC - 0xFFFD` | Fault handler                                 |
| `0xFFFE - 0xFFFF` | Reset handler                                 |

### Recommended Memory Map

The linker script recommended by default is as follows:
```
// Zero page, which may have fast access on some hardware
SECTION 0x0000 - 0x00FF : direct ;

// Stack, SADDR initialized to 0x(01)FF and decrements
SECTION 0x0100 - 0x01FF : ;

// RAM, may support software-implemented stack or heap
SECTION 0x0200 - 0x7FFF : data bss ;

// Memory-mapped IO and IO buffers
SECTION 0x8000 - 0xBFFF : ;

// Program ROM
SECTION 0xC000 - 0xFFEF : text rodata ;

// Vector table
SECTION 0xFFF0 - 0xFFFF : vectors ;
```

Which define the following sections by convention:

| Section   | Commentary                                                                                                                                                                                         |
|-----------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `direct`  | Contents to place in the first 256-byte page. This page may support faster memory operations on certain hardware implementations, and thus may be a desirable target for frequently accessed data. |
| `data`    | Initialized global data that is mutable.                                                                                                                                                           |
| `bss`     | Declared but uninitialized global data that is mutable. Runtime/startup code should initialize `bss` symbols to zero.                                                                              |
| `text`    | Executable and immutable program code.                                                                                                                                                             |
| `rodata`  | Initialized global constants.                                                                                                                                                                      |
| `vectors` | A small region for reset vector function addresses.                                                                                                                                                |

: {tbl-colwidths="[10, 90]"}

### Stack Conventions

The MISA ISA requires a towards-lower-address stack that grows towards `0x0000` on pushes and
contracts towards `0xFFFF` on pops. This convention must be respected regardless of the supported
width of the `SADDR` special register or the location in memory of the stack.

Stack operations must respect the convention of the `PUSH` and `POP` assembler macros. That is,
pushing to the stack must write before decrementing `SADDR`, and popping from the stack must
increment `SADDR` before reading.

Multi-byte pushes and pops must be logically equivalent to chaining several `PUSH` or `POP`
assembler macros.

## Reset

When the processor is taken out of the reset state, it is guaranteed by the ISA to initialize some
internal state, including:

- The reset vector address stored in memory at `0xFFFE - 0xFFFF` must be read and used to initialize
  the program counter.

The state of general purpose registers and control and status registers is implementation defined.

## Faults

Fault conditions occur when something goes wrong during program execution. This includes:

- Bad instruction decodes
- Overflow of the program counter
- Etc.

When a fault is detected, the processor must set the `CAUSE` register based on the type of fault
and then set the program counter to the fault vector address stored in memory at `0xFFFC - 0xFFFD`.
Execution must then continue in the fault handler, which is software-defined and may attempt
recovery, dump diagnostic information, or simply halt.

## Exceptions and Interrupts

The core ISA defined in this chapter does not support traditional exceptions or interrupts. The
`CAUSE` special register is intended for use as a diagnostic tool in the core architecture, and
`HALT` is the only instruction that is required to update it.

A basic synchronous exception system is supported under the System Call Extension which, when
combined with the Privilege Extension, can be used to invoke privileged routines from the
unprivileged user mode.

The Interrupt Extension provides support for basic asynchronous interrupts, which can be used to
let the processor more easily keep time and interact with peripherals.

## Base Instructions

Only 16 base instructions (with distinct opcodes and behavior) are supported by the MISA
architecture. This is a hard limit, and the 8-bit MISA architecture does not allow for more than
4 bits of opcode in each instruction word. This subsection defines all the base instructions
and their behavior on the microprocessor's state.

### `HALT`
Usage: `HALT RS`

Meaning: `CAUSE = RS << 8 | 0x01 ; exit(RS)`

Description: Halt the processor and emit the contents of `RS` for debug.

Encoding:
```{python}
#| echo: false
import wavedrom
from IPython.display import SVG
SVG(wavedrom.render(str({
    "reg": [
        *[{"name": bit, "bits": 1} for bit in reversed("0000")],
        {"name": "RS", "bits": 4},
        {"name": "Unused", "bits": 8}
    ],
    "config": {"bits": 16}
})).tostring())
```

### `ADD`
Usage: `ADD RD RS1 RS2`

Meaning: `RD = RS1 + RS2`

Description: Add the content of `RS1` and `RS2` and store the result in `RD`.

Encoding:
```{python}
#| echo: false
import wavedrom
from IPython.display import SVG
SVG(wavedrom.render(str({
    "reg": [
        *[{"name": bit, "bits": 1} for bit in reversed("0001")],
        {"name": "RD", "bits": 4},
        {"name": "RS1", "bits": 4},
        {"name": "RS2", "bits": 4}
    ],
    "config": {"bits": 16}
})).tostring())
```

### `ADC`
Usage: `ADC RD RS1 RS2`

Meaning: `RD = RS1 + RS2 + C`

Description: Add the contents of `RS1`, `RS2`, and the `C` field of the `FLAGS` register and
store the result in `RD`.

Encoding:
```{python}
#| echo: false
import wavedrom
from IPython.display import SVG
SVG(wavedrom.render(str({
    "reg": [
        *[{"name": bit, "bits": 1} for bit in reversed("0010")],
        {"name": "RD", "bits": 4},
        {"name": "RS1", "bits": 4},
        {"name": "RS2", "bits": 4}
    ],
    "config": {"bits": 16}
})).tostring())
```

### `SUB`
Usage: `SUB RD RS1 RS2`

Meaning: `RD = RS1 - RS2`

Description: Subtract the contents of `RS2` from `RS1` and store the result in `RD`.

Encoding:
```{python}
#| echo: false
import wavedrom
from IPython.display import SVG
SVG(wavedrom.render(str({
    "reg": [
        *[{"name": bit, "bits": 1} for bit in reversed("0011")],
        {"name": "RD", "bits": 4},
        {"name": "RS1", "bits": 4},
        {"name": "RS2", "bits": 4}
    ],
    "config": {"bits": 16}
})).tostring())
```

### `SBB`
Usage: `SBB RD RS1 RS2`

Meaning: `RD = RS1 + ~RS2 + C`

Description: Add the contents of `RS1`, the bitwise complement of `RS2`, and the `C` field of the
`FLAGS` register, and store the result in `RD`. Because `C` is the adder carry out, this equals
`RS1 - RS2 - (1 - C)`, so chaining `SUB` then `SBB` subtracts a multi-byte value with the borrow
carried through `C`.

Encoding:
```{python}
#| echo: false
import wavedrom
from IPython.display import SVG
SVG(wavedrom.render(str({
    "reg": [
        *[{"name": bit, "bits": 1} for bit in reversed("0100")],
        {"name": "RD", "bits": 4},
        {"name": "RS1", "bits": 4},
        {"name": "RS2", "bits": 4}
    ],
    "config": {"bits": 16}
})).tostring())
```

### `AND`
Usage: `AND RD RS1 RS2`

Meaning: `RD = RS1 & RS2`

Description: Compute the bitwise AND of the contents of `RS1` and `RS2` and store the result
in `RD`.

Encoding:
```{python}
#| echo: false
import wavedrom
from IPython.display import SVG
SVG(wavedrom.render(str({
    "reg": [
        *[{"name": bit, "bits": 1} for bit in reversed("0101")],
        {"name": "RD", "bits": 4},
        {"name": "RS1", "bits": 4},
        {"name": "RS2", "bits": 4}
    ],
    "config": {"bits": 16}
})).tostring())
```

### `OR`
Usage: `OR RD RS1 RS2`

Meaning: `RD = RS1 | RS2`

Description: Compute the bitwise OR of the contents of `RS1` and `RS2` and store the result in `RD`.

Encoding:
```{python}
#| echo: false
import wavedrom
from IPython.display import SVG
SVG(wavedrom.render(str({
    "reg": [
        *[{"name": bit, "bits": 1} for bit in reversed("0110")],
        {"name": "RD", "bits": 4},
        {"name": "RS1", "bits": 4},
        {"name": "RS2", "bits": 4}
    ],
    "config": {"bits": 16}
})).tostring())
```

### `XOR`
Usage: `XOR RD RS1 RS2`

Meaning: `RD = RS1 ^ RS2`

Description: Compute the bitwise exclusive OR of the contents of `RS1` and `RS2` and store the
result in `RD`.

Encoding:
```{python}
#| echo: false
import wavedrom
from IPython.display import SVG
SVG(wavedrom.render(str({
    "reg": [
        *[{"name": bit, "bits": 1} for bit in reversed("0111")],
        {"name": "RD", "bits": 4},
        {"name": "RS1", "bits": 4},
        {"name": "RS2", "bits": 4}
    ],
    "config": {"bits": 16}
})).tostring())
```

### `RRC`
Usage: `RRC RD RS`

Meaning: `RD = (C << 7) | (RS >> 1) ; C = RS & 1`

Description: Shift the 9-bit integer formed by `{C, RS}` right by one bit. Store the shifted
result in `RD` and the LSB of `RS` into `C`. The ALU flags are updated from the 8-bit result. `Z`
is set when the result is zero, `N` takes the most significant bit of the result, and `V` is
cleared. `C` receives the shifted-out LSB of `RS` as described above.

Encoding:
```{python}
#| echo: false
import wavedrom
from IPython.display import SVG
SVG(wavedrom.render(str({
    "reg": [
        *[{"name": bit, "bits": 1} for bit in reversed("1000")],
        {"name": "RD", "bits": 4},
        {"name": "RS", "bits": 4},
        {"name": "Unused", "bits": 4}
    ],
    "config": {"bits": 16}
})).tostring())
```

### `SET`
Usage: `SET RD IMM`

Meaning: `RD = IMM`

Description: Store the provided 8-bit immediate value into `RD`.

Encoding:
```{python}
#| echo: false
import wavedrom
from IPython.display import SVG
SVG(wavedrom.render(str({
    "reg": [
        *[{"name": bit, "bits": 1} for bit in reversed("1001")],
        {"name": "RD", "bits": 4},
        {"name": "IMM", "bits": 8}
    ],
    "config": {"bits": 16}
})).tostring())
```

### `LD`
Usage: `LD RD RS1 RS2`

Meaning: `RD = Memory[RS1 << 8 | RS2]`

Description: Load the 8-bit word at the address formed by `{RS1, RS2}` into `RD`.

Encoding:
```{python}
#| echo: false
import wavedrom
from IPython.display import SVG
SVG(wavedrom.render(str({
    "reg": [
        *[{"name": bit, "bits": 1} for bit in reversed("1010")],
        {"name": "RD", "bits": 4},
        {"name": "RS1", "bits": 4},
        {"name": "RS2", "bits": 4}
    ],
    "config": {"bits": 16}
})).tostring())
```

### `ST`
Usage: `ST RD RS1 RS2`

Meaning: `Memory[RS1 << 8 | RS2] = RD`

Description: Store the 8-bit word in `RD` to the address formed by `{RS1, RS2}`.

Encoding:
```{python}
#| echo: false
import wavedrom
from IPython.display import SVG
SVG(wavedrom.render(str({
    "reg": [
        *[{"name": bit, "bits": 1} for bit in reversed("1011")],
        {"name": "RD", "bits": 4},
        {"name": "RS1", "bits": 4},
        {"name": "RS2", "bits": 4}
    ],
    "config": {"bits": 16}
})).tostring())
```

### `RSR`
Usage: `RSR CSR RS1 RS2`

Meaning: `RS1 = CSR >> 8 ; RS2 = CSR & 0xFF`

Description: Read the 16-bit control and status register `CSR` into the two 8-bit general purpose
registers `{RS1, RS2}`

Encoding:
```{python}
#| echo: false
import wavedrom
from IPython.display import SVG
SVG(wavedrom.render(str({
    "reg": [
        *[{"name": bit, "bits": 1} for bit in reversed("1100")],
        {"name": "RS1", "bits": 4},
        {"name": "RS2", "bits": 4},
        {"name": "CSR", "bits": 4}
    ],
    "config": {"bits": 16}
})).tostring())
```

### `WSR`
Usage: `WSR CSR RS1 RS2`

Meaning: `CSR = RS1 << 8 | RS2`

Description: Write the contents formed by `{RS1, RS2}` into the 16-bit control and status
register `CSR`.

Encoding:
```{python}
#| echo: false
import wavedrom
from IPython.display import SVG
SVG(wavedrom.render(str({
    "reg": [
        *[{"name": bit, "bits": 1} for bit in reversed("1101")],
        {"name": "RS1", "bits": 4},
        {"name": "RS2", "bits": 4},
        {"name": "CSR", "bits": 4}
    ],
    "config": {"bits": 16}
})).tostring())
```

### `JAL`
Usage: `JAL CMP RS1 RS2`

Meaning: `if (CMP) { RADDR = PC + 2 ; PC = RS1 << 8 | RS2 }`

Description: If the comparison type `CMP` is true as determined by the current ALU flags, set
`RADDR` to the address of the next instruction and set `PC` to the address formed by `{RS1, RS2}`.
Note that `JAL` does not support using special registers as a branch target like `JMP` does.

Encoding:
```{python}
#| echo: false
import wavedrom
from IPython.display import SVG
SVG(wavedrom.render(str({
    "reg": [
        *[{"name": bit, "bits": 1} for bit in reversed("1110")],
        {"name": "RS1", "bits": 4},
        {"name": "RS2", "bits": 4},
        {"name": "CMP", "bits": 3},
        {"name": "Unused", "bits": 1}
    ],
    "config": {"bits": 16}
})).tostring())
```

### `JMP`
Usage: `JMP CMP RS1 RS2` or `JMP CMP CSR`

Meaning: `if (CMP) { PC = RS1 << 8 | RS2 }` or `if (CMP) { PC = CSR }`

Description: If the comparison type `CMP` is true as determined by the current ALU flags, set
`PC` to the address formed by `{RS1, RS2}` or `CSR`, whichever is provided. Jumping to the 16-bit
value in a special register is intended to be used for quickly returning to addresses like `RADDR`,
`RETSC`, and `RETIR`. The most significant bit of the instruction encoding identifies the branch
target source.

Encoding (when the branch target is stored in two general-purpose registers):
```{python}
#| echo: false
import wavedrom
from IPython.display import SVG
SVG(wavedrom.render(str({
    "reg": [
        *[{"name": bit, "bits": 1} for bit in reversed("1111")],
        {"name": "RS1", "bits": 4},
        {"name": "RS2", "bits": 4},
        {"name": "CMP", "bits": 3},
        {"name": "0", "bits": 1},
    ],
    "config": {"bits": 16}
})).tostring())
```

Encoding (when the branch target is stored in one special register):
```{python}
#| echo: false
import wavedrom
from IPython.display import SVG
SVG(wavedrom.render(str({
    "reg": [
        *[{"name": bit, "bits": 1} for bit in reversed("1111")],
        {"name": "CSR", "bits": 4},
        {"name": "Unused", "bits": 4},
        {"name": "CMP", "bits": 3},
        {"name": "1", "bits": 1},
    ],
    "config": {"bits": 16}
})).tostring())
```

## Pseudo Instructions

Because of the limitations of the core instruction set, this document also recommends a set of
assembler macros whose functionality can be represented by one or more of the base 16 instructions.

### `ADD2`
Usage: `ADD2 RD1 RD2 RS1 RS2 RS3 RS4`

Meaning: `ADD RD2 RS2 RS4`, `ADC RD1 RS1 RS3`

Description: Add the 16-bit values `{RS1, RS2}` and `{RS3, RS4}` and store the result in
`{RD1, RD2}`.

### `AND2`
Usage: `AND2 RD1 RD2 RS1 RS2 RS3 RS4`

Meaning: `AND RD2 RS2 RS4`, `AND RD1 RS1 RS3`

Description: Compute the bitwise AND of the contents of `{RS1, RS2}` and `{RS3, RS4}` and store
the result in `{RD1, RD2}`

### `CALL`
Usage: `CALL IMM`

Meaning: `SET RSCRATCH0 (IMM >> 8)`, `SET RSCRATCH1 (IMM & 0xFF)`, `JAL ALWAYS RSCRATCH0 RSCRATCH1`

Description: Jump to the subroutine at the address `IMM` and link with the `RADDR` special register.

### `CLR`
Usage: `CLR`

Meaning: `WSR FLAGS R0 R0`

Description: Set the `FLAGS` special register to zero, effectively lowering all flags.

### `CMP`
Usage: `CMP RS1 RS2`

Meaning: `SUB R0 RS1 RS2`

Description: Perform an arithmetic operation which will set the `FLAGS` register such that
the boolean operation `?` can be performed on `RS1 ? RS2`.

### `GOTO`
Usage: `GOTO IMM`

Meaning: `SET RSCRATCH0 (IMM >> 8)`, `SET RSCRATCH1 (IMM & 0xFF)`, `JMP ALWAYS RSCRATCH0 RSCRATCH1`

Description: Unconditionally jump to the address `IMM`.

### `JALI`
Usage: `JALI CMP IMM`

Meaning: `SET RSCRATCH0 (IMM >> 8)`, `SET RSCRATCH1 (IMM & 0xFF)`, `JAL CMP RSCRATCH0 RSCRATCH1`

Description: If the comparison type `CMP` is true as determined by the current ALU flags, set
`RADDR` to the address of the next instruction and set `PC` to the address `IMM`.

### `JMPI`
Usage: `JMPI CMP IMM`

Meaning: `SET RSCRATCH0 (IMM >> 8)`, `SET RSCRATCH1 (IMM & 0xFF)`, `JMP CMP RSCRATCH0 RSCRATCH1`

Description: If the comparison type `CMP` is true as determined by the current ALU flags, set
`PC` to the address `IMM`.

### `MOV`
Usage: `MOV RD RS1`

Meaning: `OR RD RS1 R0`

Description: Copy the contents of `RS1` into `RD`.

### `MOV2`
Usage: `MOV2 RD1 RD2 RS1 RS2`

Meaning: `MOV RD2 RS2`, `MOV RD1 RS1`

Description: Copy the contents of the 16-bit value `{RS1, RS2}` into `{RD1, RD2}`.

### `NOP`
Usage: `NOP`

Meaning: `OR R0 R0 R0`

Description: Do nothing.

### `OR2`
Usage: `OR2 RD1 RD2 RS1 RS2 RS3 RS4`

Meaning: `OR RD2 RS2 RS4`, `OR RD1 RS1 RS3`

Description: Compute the bitwise OR of the contents of `{RS1, RS2}` and `{RS3, RS4}` and store
the result in `{RD1, RD2}`.

### `POP`
Usage: `POP RD`

Meaning:
```
RSR SADDR RSCRATCH
SET RD 1
ADD RSCRATCH1 RSCRATCH1 RD
ADC RSCRATCH0 RSCRATCH0 R0
LD RD RSCRATCH
WSR SADDR RSCRATCH
```

Description: Increment `SADDR` by 1 byte and then load the byte at the new stack address into `RD`.

### `POP2`
Usage: `POP2 RD1 RD2`

Meaning: `POP RD1`, `POP RD2`

Description: Pop a 16-bit value off the stack and into `{RD1, RD2}`.

### `PUSH`
Usage: `PUSH RS`

Meaning:
```
RSR SADDR RSCRATCH
ST RS RSCRATCH
ADD R0 R0 R0
SBB RSCRATCH1 RSCRATCH1 R0
SBB RSCRATCH0 RSCRATCH0 R0
WSR SADDR RSCRATCH
```

Description: Write `RS` onto the stack at `SADDR`, and then decrement `SADDR` by 1 byte.

### `PUSH2`
Usage: `PUSH2 RS1 RS2`

Meaning: `PUSH RS2`, `PUSH RS1`

Description: Push a 16-bit value onto the stack from `{RS1, RS2}`.

### `RET`
Usage: `RET`

Meaning: `JMP ALWAYS RADDR`

Description: Return to the address in `RADDR`.

### `RRC2`
Usage: `RRC2 RD1 RD2 RS1 RS2`

Meaning: `RRC RD1 RS1`, `RRC RD2 RS2`

Description: Shift the 17-bit integer formed by `{C, RS1, RS2}` right by one bit. Store the shifted
result in `{RD1, RD2}` and the LSB of `RS2` into `C`.

### `SET2`
Usage: `SET2 RS1 RS2 IMM`

Meaning: `SET RS1 (IMM >> 8)`, `SET RS2 (IMM & 0xFF)`

Description: Set both the `RS1` and `RS2` registers from the high and low halves of a 16-bit
immediate value.

### `SUB2`
Usage: `SUB2 RD1 RD2 RS1 RS2 RS3 RS4`

Meaning: `SUB RD2 RS2 RS4`, `SBB RD1 RS1 RS3`

Description: Subtract the 16-bit value `{RS3, RS4}` from `{RS1, RS2}` and store the result in
`{RD1, RD2}`.

### `XOR2`
Usage: `XOR2 RD1 RD2 RS1 RS2 RS3 RS4`

Meaning: `XOR RD2 RS2 RS4`, `XOR RD1 RS1 RS3`

Description: Compute the bitwise XOR of the contents of `{RS1, RS2}` and `{RS3, RS4}` and store
the result in `{RD1, RD2}`

## Architecture Extensions

The content in this chapter until this point is the MISA core architecture. This section provides
a description of several optional extensions to that architecture which enable additional
functionalities.

### Dynamic Hardware Extension

The Dynamic Hardware Extension enables writes to the `EXTNS` special register and thus dynamic
support for the architecture extensions discussed in this section.

**Note:** If the Dynamic Hardware Extension is supported, writes to the Dynamic Hardware Extension
bit of the `EXTNS` special register must always be ignored. The extension cannot be used to disable
itself at runtime.

If the Dynamic Hardware Extension is not supported, writes to any bit of `EXTNS` are ignored. The
list of supported extensions is static and a property of the hardware itself. If supported, writes
must take effect on the instruction following the `WSR`.

Partial support of the Dynamic Hardware Extension is also allowed. That is, an implementation may
only permit enabling/disabling specific, but not every extension at runtime. In that case, writes
to the bit of any extension that cannot be toggled must be ignored. Software should treat the lack
of change in the target bit as a signal that the target extension is permanently enabled/disabled.

### System Call Extension

The System Call Extension extends the `HALT` instruction in the core architecture to support basic
synchronous exceptions that may be used for system calls and other similar features.

#### `SYSCALL`
The `SYSCALL` instruction replaces the `HALT` instruction in the assembler under the System Call
Extension. Its usage is similar to `HALT`, but with a conditional "exception" bit that controls
the terminal behavior of the processor.

Usage: `SYSCALL RS`

Meaning:
```
CAUSE = RS << 8 | 0x01
if (E == 0) { exit(RS) } else { PC = Memory[0xFFFB] << 8 | Memory[0xFFFA] }
```

Encoding:
```{python}
#| echo: false
import wavedrom
from IPython.display import SVG
SVG(wavedrom.render(str({
    "reg": [
        *[{"name": bit, "bits": 1} for bit in reversed("0000")],
        {"name": "RS", "bits": 4},
        {"name": "Unused", "bits": 7},
        {"name": "E", "bits": 1}
    ],
    "config": {"bits": 16}
})).tostring())
```

#### `HALT`
`HALT` functionality as defined in the core architecture is supported under the System Call
Extension by setting the `E` bit to `0`. In that case, the processor must adhere to the core
architecture behavior for `HALT`, including stopping the clock and setting the `CAUSE` register.

#### Calling Conventions and Stack Frame
When a `SYSCALL` instruction is executed, the contents of the `RS` register are used as the syscall
code, stored in the `CAUSE` special register. The syscall handler address at `0xFFFA - 0xFFFB` is
responsible for reading the `CAUSE` register, understanding that a syscall was executed, and
using the extended status value to branch to different handler code for each type of call.

General purpose registers follow the same caller-callee conventions as standard subroutine/function
calls in the MISA ABI. This includes which registers are used as arguments to the system call, and
which registers are used as return values from the system call. All special registers must be
saved and restored by the system call routine.

#### Nested System Calls
The `SYSCALL` instruction may not be executed within a system call context. The processor is
canonically in a system call context under the following formal definition:

- The processor enters a system call context when the `SYSCALL` instruction is executed with the
  exception bit set
- The processor leaves the system call context when a `JMP ALWAYS RETSC` instruction is executed
- Every instruction executed between entering and leaving the system call context exists within the
  system call context
  
If a secondary `SYSCALL` is performed in a system call context, a fault must occur with the
`CAUSE` Reason "Control event" and the `CAUSE` Type "Improper system call".

#### Returning From System Calls
To return from system calls, the `RETSC` special register is defined, which stores the return
address when a `SYSCALL` instruction is executed.

```{python}
#| echo: false
import wavedrom
from IPython.display import SVG
SVG(wavedrom.render(str({
    "reg": [
        {"name": "RETSC", "bits": 16},
    ],
    "config": {"bits": 16}
})).tostring())
```

The following pseudo-instruction is defined to return to this address easily:

Usage: `RETS`

Meaning: `JMP ALWAYS RETSC`

Description: Return from a system call to the address in `RETSC`.

### Interrupt Extension

The Interrupt Extension adds support for basic asynchronous, non-deterministic exceptions. While
the synchronous exceptions in the System Call Extension come from code being executed by the
processor, interrupts are triggered externally to allow the processor to keep time, communicate
with peripherals, and more.

#### Triggering Interrupts
MISA processors supporting the interrupt extension must designate one pin as the interrupt pin. This
specification does not define whether the interrupt pin is active-high or active-low. The interrupt
pin is set to its active state when an interrupt occurs, and rising or falling edge must cause the
processor to finish executing the current instruction and then set the program counter to the
interrupt handler address at `0xFFF8 - 0xFFF9`.

When this happens, interrupts must be automatically disabled by the processor. If the interrupt pin
is toggled, another interrupt should not be detected. Taking interrupts does not affect the `CAUSE`
register like system calls or faults.

#### Interrupt Queue
Information about which interrupt was triggered is provided to the processor through a memory-mapped
queue. This specification does not define whether the queue should be located in memory.

The queue is structured as follows:

| Bytes | Purpose             |
|-------|---------------------|
| 0     | Length              |
| 1     | Pop signal          |
| 2     | Pop acknowledgement |
| 3     | Interrupt number    |
| 4-5   | Argument pointer    |

Every field except for the pop signal may only be read by the processor. Writing to other fields
is undefined behavior.

The length field defines the number of outstanding interrupts. The interrupt handler should respond
to every interrupt in the queue before returning, as it is not guaranteed that the interrupt source
will reassert the interrupt pin. If the queue is not emptied before returning, interrupts will be
left unaddressed until the next time the pin is asserted.

When responding to an interrupt, the interrupt handler should read the number and argument pointer
fields, and then pop the entry using the pop handshake.

The pop handshake uses the pop signal and pop acknowledgement fields as request and acknowledge
signals. The pop signal is written by the processor to any non-zero value when the current interrupt
should be popped from the queue. The pop acknowledgement is written by the external hardware to any
non-zero value when the requested pop is completed and the queue fields are updated. Both fields are
zero in the idle state, including after reset and when the Interrupt Extension is first enabled.

The handshake proceeds in four phases. To pop an entry, the processor must:

1. Write a non-zero value to the pop signal to request the pop.
2. Wait until the pop acknowledgement is non-zero.
3. Write zero to the pop signal to withdraw the request.
4. Wait until the pop acknowledgement is zero before beginning another pop.

In response, the external hardware must:

1. On the pop signal becoming non-zero, remove the head entry, update the length and (if the queue is
   not empty) the number and argument pointer fields to reflect the new head, and only then write a
   non-zero value to the pop acknowledgement.
2. On the pop signal returning to zero, write zero to the pop acknowledgement.

The fourth phase is required. Without waiting for the pop acknowledgement to return to zero, a
subsequent pop could observe the acknowledgement left over from the previous pop and read stale head
fields.

While the handshake is idle (both the pop signal and pop acknowledgement are zero) and the length is
non-zero, the number and argument pointer fields must hold the head entry. To preserve this, the
external hardware must modify those fields only during a pop (between observing the pop signal
non-zero and asserting the pop acknowledgement) or, when enqueuing into an empty queue, before
incrementing the length. The processor must read those fields only while the handshake is idle and
the length is non-zero.

The exact use of the interrupt number and argument pointer fields are implementation-defined. The
intent is for the interrupt handler to dispatch to a specific service routine based on the number,
passing the argument pointer as a pointer to a particular type of structure containing information
for the service routine. When the length of the queue is zero, the values of the interrupt number
and argument pointer are undefined.

#### Calling Conventions
Because interrupts are not necessarily triggered by the running code in the way system calls are,
the entire processor state is considered to be callee-saved in an interrupt context. The interrupt
handler is responsible for saving and restoring every special and general purpose register that it
modifies.

Three exceptions are the `RSCRATCH0` and `RSCRATCH1` general-purpose registers, and the `FLAGS`
special register. These registers must be automatically saved by the processor when an interrupt is
triggered and automatically restored when returning from the interrupt. On entry, `RSCRATCH` is
therefore the only register the handler may freely use before saving anything; every other register
still holds the interrupted program's live data.

#### Returning From Interrupts
To return from interrupts, the `RETIR` special register is defined, which stores the return address
when an interrupt is triggered.

```{python}
#| echo: false
import wavedrom
from IPython.display import SVG
SVG(wavedrom.render(str({
    "reg": [
        {"name": "RETIR", "bits": 16},
    ],
    "config": {"bits": 16}
})).tostring())
```

The following pseudo-instruction is defined to return to this address easily:

Usage: `RETI`

Meaning: `JMP ALWAYS RETIR`

Description: Return from an interrupt to the address in `RETIR`.

When the processor executes `JMP ALWAYS RETIR`, it must also perform the following actions
atomically:

1. Restore `RSCRATCH0`, `RSCRATCH1`, `FLAGS`, and `PRIVS.R` (under the Privilege Extension)
2. Set the program counter to the address in `RETIR`
3. Leave the interrupt context and reenable interrupts

Software must not return from an interrupt via `RSR RETIR RSCRATCH; JMP ALWAYS RSCRATCH`, as this
is not guaranteed to complete steps 1 and 3.

#### Masking Interrupts

Interrupt masking may not be controlled by software. If the Interrupt Extension is supported,
interrupts may always be triggered. Only two conditions prevent the processor from taking new
interrupts:

1. Disabling the Interrupt Extension through the Dynamic Hardware Extension.
2. Being in an interrupt context.

The processor is canonically in an interrupt context under the following formal definition:

- The processor enters an interrupt context when the program counter is set to the address of the
  interrupt handler as a result of the interrupt pin going active
- The processor leaves an interrupt context when a `JMP ALWAYS RETIR` instruction is executed
- Every instruction executed between entering and leaving the interrupt context exists within the
  interrupt context

Software may choose to ignore the interrupt by returning immediately from the interrupt handler.

#### System Calls in Interrupts
While the processor is in an interrupt context, system calls may not be executed. If a system call
is performed in an interrupt context, the processor must fault with the reason "Control event"
and the type "Improper system call".

#### Canonical Interrupt Handler
With `RSCRATCH` and `FLAGS` saved by the processor, interrupt handlers are free to modify them. One
method of saving and restoring the full context in the interrupt handler is as follows:

```asm
Interrupt_Handler:
    PUSH2 RAB
    PUSH2 RCD
    ...                         ; Save other general purpose registers

    RSR RADDR RAB
    PUSH2 RAB
    ...                         ; Save other special registers

    ;; Read the interrupt queue, dispatch a service routine, drain the queue

    ...                         ; Restore other special registers
    POP2 RAB
    WSR RADDR RAB

    ...                         ; Restore other general purpose registers
    POP2 RCD
    POP2 RAB

    RETI                        ; Return from the interrupt
```

### Privilege Extension

The Privilege Extension segments the capabilities of the processor into two distinct levels of
privilege, which can be used to limit the actions taken by untrusted software.

Machine Mode grants access to all functionality of the processor, and is similar in scope to the
core architecture without the Privilege Extension. User Mode restricts access to certain features
of the core architecture, and provides a way to manage memory I/O at a more cautious level of
privilege.

#### `PRIVS`

Privilege is tracked and controlled using the `PRIVS` special register, which is defined as part of
the Privilege Extension. It is a flags register with the following fields:

| Flag | Bit | Commentary                                                   |
|------|-----|--------------------------------------------------------------|
| `R`  | 0   | The privilege ring bit. 0 for Machine Mode, 1 for User Mode. |

```{python}
#| echo: false
import wavedrom
from IPython.display import SVG
SVG(wavedrom.render(str({
    "reg": [
        {"name": "R", "bits": 1},
        {"name": "Reserved (optional)", "bits": 15}
    ],
    "config": {"bits": 16}
})).tostring())
```

#### User Mode Restrictions

When the processor is in User Mode, the following actions must cause a privilege-related fault:

- Execution of `HALT`
- Execution of `RSR` except on `SADDR`, `RADDR`, `FLAGS`, and `PRIVS`
- Execution of `WSR` except on `SADDR`, `RADDR`, and `FLAGS`
- Access to privileged memory, if a memory protection unit is used to manage access based on the
  ring bit

If a privilege error is detected, the processor must preempt the instruction which caused the error,
discard any partial result of the instruction, and jump to the fault handler. The `CAUSE` special
register must be set to indicate the privilege error for the instruction use or memory access.

#### Points of Privilege Change

Under normal operation, the processor is expected to change privilege modes when the following
occur:

- When any fault occurs which requires the processor to jump to the fault handler (including an
  User Mode privilege error), the processor must first set `PRIVS.R` to 0.
- Under the System Call Extension, when the `SYSCALL` instruction is executed and the exception
  bit is 1, `PRIVS.R` must be set to 0 before the system call handler is entered.
- Under the System Call Extension, when the processor is returned from a system call context, the
  `PRIVS.R` bit must be restored to its initial value before the `SYSCALL`.
- Under the Interrupt Extension, when an interrupt is taken, `PRIVS.R` must be set to 0 before the
  interrupt handler is entered.
- Under the Interrupt Extension, when the processor is returned from an interrupt context, the
  `PRIVS.R` bit must be restored to its initial value before the interrupt occurred. Note that
  interrupts may trigger while the processor is in a system call context, in which case returning
  from the interrupt and returning from the system call will restore different ring bit values.
- When `WSR` is executed on the `PRIVS` special register from Machine Mode, the updated ring
  bit must take effect for the next instruction.

All privilege changes must be performed automatically by the processor when an appropriate condition
is detected, except for direct writes to `PRIVS` via `WSR` from Machine Mode.
